name: Shirley Heights
label: Shirley Heights
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Blockhouse' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Blockhouse' (node/4621518007): point.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Hilltop lookout over English Harbour, famous for its sunset views.

text.description: Shirley Heights is a popular high viewpoint in Antigua, and it works for a phone camera because the land drops away so far below you. The classic picture is from the Shirley Heights Lookout, with English Harbour and Falmouth Harbour spread out beneath you, yacht masts in the water and the coastline curling round. For something a little different, go to The Blockhouse, a viewpoint at the largest fortress on the site. It faces the east coast, so it suits an early start: you can catch the sunrise over the water, usually with fewer people around than at the main lookout. Shirley Heights gets very busy on Sunday evenings, when the parties are crowded, and weekday mornings are calmer for photos. If you want a sunset instead, Dow's Hill Interpretation Centre gives a view of the sun going down close to the line of English Harbour. One guide says it closes around 5pm and the fence view is hard to reach, so it may not be available at sunset. Bring a light layer for an early start, keep your lens clean, and take a few frames both wide and zoomed in, because the coast looks different at each setting.
text.geographic_location: Shirley Heights overlooks English Harbour and Falmouth Harbour in Antigua. The Blockhouse is part of the same fortress site as the main lookout.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops on Antigua, so head for English Harbour and get up to Shirley Heights by road; check local options before you go. Once you are on the site, follow the signs to the main lookout, and The Blockhouse is elsewhere on the same site, reached on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of coast and sky, then use the default lens (1x) for a natural view. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the fortress walls, boats or a stretch of coastline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (viewpoint at the largest fortress, facing the east coast). Antigua's east coast and the sunrise over it, as a quieter alternative to the main lookout. The Shirley Heights Lookout is elsewhere on the same site and can be reached on foot, so walk over there for the harbour view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the horizon on the top or bottom line so the sea stays level. Include a bit of the fortress stonework in the foreground to give the view some depth. If you can, also take the classic shot from Shirley Heights Lookout, with English Harbour and Falmouth Harbour and the yacht masts below.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunrise colours do not wash out. Take a Live Photo too: moving clouds or flags can make a nice short clip. If the light is still dim before sunrise, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise at The Blockhouse. Weekday mornings are calmer than Sunday evenings. For sunset, the Dow's Hill Interpretation Centre view is an option, but check it is open first.

text.access_note: Shirley Heights is part of a national park site where an entry fee may apply, and what you pay may vary by day and time, so check the official site before you go.

name: Sir Vivian Richards Stadium
label: Vivian Richards Stadiu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sir Vivian Richards Stadium' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/19881528: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sir Vivian Richards Stadium' (610 m across).
notes: International cricket ground built for the 2007 World Cup.

text.description:
Sir Vivian Richards Stadium is Antigua's international cricket ground, named after the former West Indies captain Viv Richards. For a phone photographer the best picture here is not the whole stadium but the bronze statue of Viv Richards raising his bat, which stands outside the main entrance in front of the pavilion. It gives you a person, a pose and a recognisable building in a single frame. The statue stands outside the pavilion entrance and is easy to frame without going inside, but it is unclear whether an entry fee applies, so check on the day.

The stadium was built for the 2007 Cricket World Cup and usually holds about 10,000 people, though temporary seating doubled that for the tournament. It has two main stands, the Northern Stand and the five-storey South Stand, and it has since hosted Test matches and, in 2024, matches of the ICC Men's T20 World Cup. It sits in the North Sound area of Saint George parish, roughly a 10-20 minute drive from St. John's.

The ground is large, so keep your framing simple. Stand back far enough to fit the whole statue, with the raised bat clear against the sky or the pavilion behind. Keep the statue in the centre or on one third of the frame, and try a second shot from a little lower down so the figure looks taller. Check for people walking through the picture before you press the shutter. Entrance rules and match-day restrictions can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In North Sound, in the parish of Saint George, Antigua. It is roughly a 10-20 minute drive from St. John's and the airport.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this spot. The stadium is about a 10-20 minute drive from St. John's and can be reached from the Sir Sydney Walling Highway. Once at the stadium, head for the main entrance and the pavilion, where the statue stands. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with the entrance and pavilion behind it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more of the building, and keep the statue near the middle so it is not stretched at the edges. The telephoto (2x or more) is good for a tighter shot of the raised bat and the face.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then stand back far enough to fit the whole statue, with the stadium entrance and pavilion behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, leaving the pavilion visible behind it. Crouch slightly and hold the phone low and level so the raised bat sits against the sky. Wait for a gap in passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the bronze keeps its detail instead of turning into a dark silhouette. Portrait mode is not needed for a statue, and may blur the edges oddly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is behind you or off to one side so the statue is lit rather than a silhouette. Check the stadium's official site for events, as match days may be busier and have different rules.

text.access_note: The statue is outside the pavilion entrance, but it is unclear whether an entry fee applies for the statue spot, and access may be restricted at times, so check on the day and on the official site before you go.

name: Nelson's Dockyard
label: Nelson's Dockyard
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shirley Heights' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Shirley Heights' (node/5435642864): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2293555115: the OpenStreetMap point 'Nelson's Dockyards National Park'.
notes: Restored Georgian naval dockyard at English Harbour, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

text.description:
Nelson's Dockyard sits around English Harbour on Antigua's south coast, and it is the only Georgian-era dockyard in the world that still works as a dockyard. The Royal Navy built it up in the 18th century and left in 1889. It is named after Admiral Horatio Nelson, who lived there from 1784 to 1787. Restoration began in 1951 and the site reopened to the public in 1961. Today the old storehouses, workshops and officers' quarters share the waterfront with a marina, shops, restaurants and a museum. It is part of Nelson's Dockyard National Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The best overall photo is not taken inside the dockyard but from above it, on Shirley Heights. From the lookout you see the dockyard below, English Harbour in the foreground, and Falmouth Harbour and the coastline stretching away beyond. Guides call it the classic panoramic view, and it works well on a phone because the scene is so wide. Look for the line of old buildings along the water, the yachts at anchor, and the layers of hills and sea behind them.

If you want a different angle, Dow's Hill Interpretation Centre gives a wide view over the whole national park. Fort Berkeley has old stone walls and cannon positions that frame the coast, with fewer people around. On Sunday evenings the Shirley Heights barbecue parties are lively and photogenic but crowded, so arrive early if you want a clear spot at the railing.
text.geographic_location: The dockyard is at English Harbour on the south coast of Antigua, in the parish of Saint Paul.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops here, so start from English Harbour and go on foot (a short hike) or by taxi to Shirley Heights. On foot it is a short hike, mostly uphill. Once there, face north-west and the dockyard lies below you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the dockyard, both harbours and the coastline in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view of the dockyard and harbour. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the old buildings and yachts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Shirley Heights (lookout above English Harbour, looking down on the dockyard). Nelson's Dockyard below with English Harbour in the foreground and Falmouth Harbour and the coastline beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top third line so the harbour and dockyard fill most of the frame. Use the railing or a foreground edge to add depth, and keep the horizon level. For a different view, try Dow's Hill Interpretation Centre for the whole national park, or Fort Berkeley for old stone walls and cannon positions framing the coast.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dockyard to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode for the full sweep of the two harbours, moving slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset gives the best light, according to the photography guides. Sunday evenings are lively but crowded.

text.access_note: Shirley Heights is a public lookout, but fees may apply to the Blockhouse and the dockyard itself, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Shirley Heights lies roughly south-east of the dockyard and is a climb from English Harbour on foot.
Late-afternoon sun is low in the west, so the scene will be lit from the side and the sky can be bright when looking north-west.

name: Jolly Harbour
label: Jolly Harbour
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jolly Beach' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jolly Beach' (way/35966870): edge nearest the subject (1368 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Jolly Harbour'.
notes: Marina and resort community on the west coast.

text.description: Jolly Harbour is a neighbourhood of Bolans on Antigua's southwest coast, and the main beach in the area is Jolly Beach: a long curve of white sand and turquoise water on Lignum Vitae Bay. Standing at the southern public end gives the widest sweep of the beach, and you can frame it without resort buildings in the shot. The area has a surprising past. Jolly Beach is among the oldest Archaic period sites in the Leeward Islands, with artefacts dated to between about 1775 BC and 1589 BC. Before the 1980s the harbour area was swampy mangrove, and today it is a busy marina with shops, bars and restaurants. That mix gives you two quite different photos in one visit: a clean, open beach view, and a sheltered marina basin with yachts and sailboats moored in front of the shoreline. The simplest plan is to start with the beach, then walk towards the marina for a second set of pictures. Keep the horizon level, let the sand curve lead the eye into the frame, and take a few shots at slightly different heights for variety. The resort frontage along the beach can work as a backdrop, but it is resort property, so be sensible about where you stand. If you fly a drone, check the local rules first.
text.geographic_location: Jolly Harbour is on the southwest coast of Antigua, in Saint Mary Parish, in the Bolans community. It lies east of Lignum Vitae Bay and south of the Pearns Point peninsula.
text.directions_text: There is no train or tram here. Road access is via Valley Road. Jolly Harbour is about 7.5 km from St John's and about 1.3 km from central Bolans, which is roughly 15 minutes on foot (an estimate). Once you reach the neighbourhood, head for the southern public end of Jolly Beach, which is the recommended viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full sweep of sand and sea. The default lens (1x) is better for a calmer, more natural view, and the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) helps pick out boats at the marina.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (southern public end of the beach). The full stretch of white sand and turquoise water, with no resort buildings in the frame. The harbour and marina lie off to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, with the waterline curving through the picture. Keep the sea level and let the beach lead into the distance. For a second option, try the marina with yachts and sailboats moored in the basin and the shoreline behind them. You can also use the resort frontage as a backdrop with the beach and water in front, but access there may depend on the resort.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky or sea to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little to keep the colour in the water and the sand from turning white. Try a Live Photo as the waves roll in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Just after sunrise, or before 8am, for cleaner light and an emptier beach.

text.access_note: The southern end of Jolly Beach is a public part of the beach, but the resort frontage is private property, so check the official site before you go if you plan to shoot from there.

name: Fort James
label: Fort James
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fort James Beach' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W1031834593 (Fort James): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Ruined 18th-century fort guarding the entrance to St. John's Harbour.

text.description:
Fort James is a largely ruined fort by the sea, and its charm is in the details: old stone walls, cannons and big old trees, with the harbour and the Caribbean Sea beyond. It is a relaxed place to take pictures rather than a polished attraction. There is little signage on site, and you may see some litter and marine debris, so choose your angles with that in mind.

The phone icon on the map is at the fort itself. From the walls you can put the cannons and crumbling stonework in the foreground and the harbour and sea behind them.

For a different view, try Fort James Beach as an alternative. The beach runs right up to the site, and from the sand you can look up at the ruined walls and cannons, with palms and sand filling the foreground. This spot is not the map's phone-icon location, so walk a little along the sand and try a few positions before settling on one.

Keep your pictures simple: one strong foreground (a palm, a patch of wall or a cannon), then the stonework behind it. Check the lens and screen for sand and salt spray before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Fort James stands on the coast of Antigua, with a beach running right up to the site.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are listed for this spot. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is at the fort itself. Fort James Beach, beside the site, is a separate alternative viewpoint. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the walls, palms and sand together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the beach and the fort in one frame, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a cannon or a section of stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Put the cannons and crumbling stonework in the foreground, with the harbour and sea behind. For an alternative view, walk to Fort James Beach and look up at the walls and old trees from the sand, with palms and sand in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place a cannon or a patch of stonework in the lower part of the frame, with the harbour and sea behind it. If you try the beach alternative, place the line of the walls along the upper third, with the sand and a palm filling the lower part. Crouch slightly to make the walls look taller and to keep any litter out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone does not wash out. Wipe the lens first, as sea air can leave a haze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day, when the sun is lower, usually gives softer light on the stonework and less glare on the sand.

name: Devil's Bridge
label: Devil's Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Devil's Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W54584998 (Devil's Bridge): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Natural limestone arch with blowholes on the Atlantic coast.

text.description:
Devil's Bridge is a natural limestone arch on Antigua's Atlantic coast, where the waves push through and under the rock and send spray up from the blowholes nearby. That moving water is what makes it work so well on a phone: the pale rock, the dark blue sea and the white foam give you strong contrast and plenty going on in the frame.

The classic photo is taken from the clifftop and rocky ledges above the arch, not from the bridge itself. From there you see the arch in profile with waves breaking through it. Guides describe this as the standard Devil's Bridge picture, and early morning is recommended for the best colour. On breezier days the blowholes are livelier, so you may get extra spray in the shot.

Take care here. The rock is very slippery and the waves are unpredictable, so stay well back from the edge and do not walk out onto the arch. One guide says it is not meant for walking. The access road is unpaved and bumpy, so allow extra time to get there.

If you want a quieter, wider shot, Indian Town Point on the nearby coastal path shows the rugged shoreline and the bridge area. It may not give a direct view of the arch, so check when you arrive. Wherever you shoot, keep both feet on solid ground and let the zoom do the work.
text.geographic_location: Devil's Bridge is on Antigua's Atlantic coast, in the Indian Town area, on the clifftop beside the rocky shoreline and the nearby blowholes.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near here; head for the Indian Town area. The access road to the arch is unpaved and bumpy, so go slowly. The phone icon on the map is right at the arch. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the arch in profile with the waves passing under it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole rugged coastline. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out spray and the arch from a safe distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at Devil's Bridge on the clifftop and rocky ledges above the arch, not on the bridge itself. Keep well back from the edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arch on one third of the frame, with the horizon level along a top or bottom line. Let the waves fill the gap under the arch. Try a Live Photo so you can pick the best moment as a wave breaks. For a different view, Indian Town Point on the coastal path shows a wider stretch of shoreline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale rock to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white foam and bright sky keep their detail. Use Live Photos/motion to catch the spray, and hold the phone with both hands on slippery ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, for the best colour on the rock and water. Breezy days make the blowholes more active.

text.access_note: The rock is very slippery and the waves are unpredictable, so stay well back from the edge. The official name varies between guides, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Devil's Bridge and Indian Town are on the eastern side of Antigua.
Spray from the sea can get on a phone lens, so wipe it with a dry cloth before shooting.
Telephoto (2x-5x) lets you frame the arch from a safe distance back from the edge.

name: Half Moon Bay
label: Half Moon Bay
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Half Moon Bay' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N426020007 (Half Moon Bay): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Crescent-shaped beach on the Atlantic side in a national park.

text.description: Half Moon Bay is a curved beach on Antigua's Atlantic side, set inside a national park. It photographs well because the shape does the work for you: a sweeping crescent of pink-tinged sand, turquoise water, and surf rolling in along the whole length of the beach. The best frame comes from the small, rugged headland at the north end. From up there you look back down the beach and can see the half-moon curve, with the waves breaking on the sand. A little height also lets the whole crescent fit into one frame, so it suits a phone well. The ruins of an abandoned hotel stand against the treeline, which gives a useful second subject if you want something other than sea and sand. Wear shoes with a good grip, because the short climb up the headland is a scramble and the path is rough. The surf is strong, so keep well back from the water's edge and from any drop while you are lining up a shot. Take your time, check your footing before you raise the phone, and take a few frames from both the sand and the headland so you can compare them later.
text.geographic_location: Half Moon Bay is on the Atlantic coast of Antigua, within a national park. The beach is backed by trees.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed near Half Moon Bay, so you will need to arrange road transport to the beach on Antigua's Atlantic coast. Ask the driver for Half Moon Bay beach. Once there, walk to the north end of the beach and head for the northern headland near the phone icon on the map. The headland is not named on the map, so locate the best spot on the ground. It is a short scramble, so take care on the rough ground. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) from the headland so the whole crescent of sand and water fits in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the breaking surf or the ruins against the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face back down the bay so the curve of the sand and the Atlantic surf breaking on it fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the curve of the shoreline along one of the lower lines, with the sea in the top third and the sand in the bottom. Keep the horizon level. If you have time, take a second frame from the top of the access path, where the whole crescent also fits in one shot. A low sun on the sand also shows up the pink tint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sand to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white surf keeps its detail and the turquoise stays rich. Try a Live Photo to catch the waves rolling in, and wipe the lens first, as sea spray is likely.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Low morning sun lights the pink tint in the sand and the calm, reflective turquoise water, while the ruins sit against the treeline.

text.access_note: The bay is inside a national park and the headland path is rough, so check the official site before you go for any access rules.

name: Boggy Peak
label: Boggy Peak
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Boggy Peak' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/206147469: the OpenStreetMap point 'Boggy Peak'.
notes: Highest point on Antigua, in the southwest hills.

text.description: Boggy Peak is the highest point on Antigua, at 1,319 feet (402 m), in the Shekerley Mountains in the southwest of the island. It is a viewpoint rather than a pretty summit. The top is taken up by a fenced communications compound, so the photo you want is of the land spread out below it. From the rocky edge outside the fence you can see the western and southern parts of Antigua, with Jolly Harbour in the view, and the compound's masts and fencing make a useful foreground. The name has a history: it was changed to Mount Obama in 2009 and restored to Boggy Peak in 2016, so you may see either on signs and in guidebooks. The slopes were once sugarcane plantations worked by enslaved people, and the name is said to come from bogeyman stories told to discourage escape. That is worth remembering when you stand up here. Trees, masts and cables can get in the way, so move a few steps along the rocks until your frame is clear. Take one wide shot to show how high you are, then a closer one of the harbour and coast. A cloudy or hazy day flattens the view, so pick a clear one. The ground is rocky and the approach is steep, so wear proper shoes and keep well back from any drop.
text.geographic_location: Boggy Peak is in the far southwest of Antigua, at the top of the Shekerley Mountains, looking down towards Jolly Harbour and the west coast.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or train service here. The summit can be reached by a 4x4 road or on foot on a steep hike, for example from Christian Valley, Cades Bay or Morris Bay, or from the Jennings Road side. Ask your driver or hotel which approach suits your vehicle and fitness. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the big sweep of coast and hills with the compound in front. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Jolly Harbour and the bays in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Go to the right of the gates and follow the wall round. From here the communications compound is in the foreground, with the western and southern parts of Antigua and Jolly Harbour below. Stay outside the fence; you do not need to go in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line so the land below fills the frame. Let the fence and masts sit at one edge as a foreground, and move along the rocks to keep cables and tree branches out of the shot. For a second picture, zoom in on the harbour and its coastline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the distant coast to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the land does not go pale. Use panorama only if you can hold the phone level and steady, away from the fence.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, as cloud and haze flatten the view. Mornings and late afternoon usually give softer light on the landscape, but leave enough daylight for the steep walk down.

text.access_note: The summit is a fenced communications compound whose gate is sometimes locked, so stay on the rocky ground outside it, and check locally before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Mornings and late afternoon usually give softer light for landscape views.
A clear day gives a better view than a cloudy or hazy one.
The viewing edge is rocky and the approach is steep, so sturdy shoes and care near drops are sensible.
Using the ultra-wide, the default lens (1x) and telephoto each suit a different part of the view.

name: Fort Barrington
label: Fort Barrington
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Deep Bay Beach' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Deep Bay Beach' (way/35966767): middle (511 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W345312485 (Fort Barrington): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Hilltop fort with a view over St. John's Harbour and Deep Bay.

text.description:
Fort Barrington is a ruined hilltop fort above Deep Bay, overlooking St. John's Harbour. The best-known phone shot is from the sand of Deep Bay Beach, looking up. Photographing it from below like this gives a sense of height that is hard to get once you are up at the walls.

The beach is a public one. The trail up to the fort starts from the beach side, so you can take the shot from the sand first and decide afterwards whether to climb. The path is steep and unimproved, ropes help on the steepest sections, and there is little shade. Wear closed shoes and keep one hand free for the phone and one for the rope.

If you do go up, the fort itself looks over St. John's Harbour, Deep Bay and the open Caribbean, with the ruins in the foreground. A quieter alternative is Fort Barrington National Park, which has a view of the coastline and the small offshore rock with the fort behind you.

Take your photos from the sand first, while your phone and your hands are steady, then walk up. Keep your phone in a pocket or a wrist strap on the climb.
text.geographic_location: Fort Barrington stands on the hill at the head of Deep Bay, on Antigua.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops nearby. The beach is reached via the car park and the trail from it. Reviews warn of break-ins at the parking area, so go early and leave nothing visible in the car. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the walls above the beach and bay. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the hill and shoreline in the frame, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the ramparts against the slope.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Deep Bay Beach (sand at the foot of the hill, looking up at the fort; the trail starts from the beach side). The fort's walls and ramparts rising above the shoreline and the bay, framed from below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the fort's walls on the upper third line, with the bay or shoreline filling the lower part so the ruin looks high above the water. Keep the phone level so the horizon and hillside don't tilt. If you climb up, an alternative is to shoot from Fort Barrington National Park, where you look along the coastline to the small offshore rock with the fort behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone walls to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky and sea don't wash out. A Live Photo can catch the movement of the waves in front of the fort. Use panorama from the top for the harbour and bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early, as reviews warn of break-ins at the car park, and leave nothing visible in the car.

text.access_note: The site is free and open-air, with no formal fee, though one listing mentions a possible small parking fee, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Panorama mode suits the view of the harbour and bay from the top of the hill.
A Live Photo can capture wave movement in front of the fort.

name: Betty's Hope
label: Betty's Hope
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Betty's Hope' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2912539: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Restored 17th-century sugar plantation with twin windmill towers.

text.description: Betty's Hope was the first large sugar plantation on Antigua, set up in 1650 and run by the Codrington family from 1674 until 1944. Today it is a quiet, open-air heritage site in rolling limestone countryside, and the ruins make good subjects for a phone camera. The twin stone windmills are the usual photo. One has been restored with its wooden sails, which stay mounted all year, though they turn only on special occasions. The old Still House, once the rum distillery, is a roofless ruin with elegant arches, and it makes a calmer and more textured picture. Plants have crept over the stone, and the arches frame the sky and the open grounds. Fewer people tend to photograph it than the mills. The buildings have been an open-air museum with a visitor centre since 1995, managed by the Museum of Antigua and Barbuda. Walk around the site before you shoot. Start in the Still House for the arches and texture, then step outside for the windmill with its sails against the sky. Keep to the outside of the restored mill, as access to its interior has been restricted. Because this was a place where enslaved people worked for centuries, a calm, respectful approach suits the site. Wear sturdy shoes, as the approach is a dirt track.
text.geographic_location: Betty's Hope lies in the Diamonds area of Antigua, in open rural country just south of the village of Pares.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops here, so head for the village of Pares first. From the centre of Pares the site is about 15 to 20 minutes on foot, along a dirt track off the Pares Village Main Road, heading south. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the Still House to take in the full sweep of the arches. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the windmill and its sails. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the stonework and plants.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Go inside the roofless Still House ruin, enter from the back, and shoot through the arched walls. The photo shows the overgrown stone arches framing the sky and the open grounds beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up one arch so it frames the sky, keeping the walls level on both sides. For a second picture, stand outside and use the default lens (1x) to put the restored windmill and its sails against open sky, with the ruins around it. This is the more usual shot, and the Still House is the quieter alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out. If your phone has an HDR option, leave it on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit in the early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: Access to the site is informal and the visitor centre is often closed, so don't count on it being open, and shoot the restored windmill from outside.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light for photographs in Antigua.
Bright sky seen through a shaded ruin can look washed out unless you lower the exposure.

name: St. John's Cathedral
label: St. John's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Newgate Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Newgate Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W35763185 (St. John's Cathedral): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Twin-towered Anglican cathedral overlooking St. John's.

text.description:
St. John's Cathedral is the big church with twin towers that anchors this part of town, and its west front is the picture most visitors want. A travel guide names this street as the best place to photograph the cathedral, and it is the usual choice for the full front view. That is the classic postcard framing, and it works well on a phone because the symmetry of the towers does most of the job for you.

For a quieter, more atmospheric alternative, the cathedral grounds and old cemetery park show the church among 18th- and 19th-century tombstones and greenery. One guide says the only open gate is on Long Street, so check the official site before you go.

The exterior and grounds were still being restored as of 2023, so you may see scaffolding in your shots. If it spoils the view, try a tighter crop on one tower, or take a second frame from the grounds. Keep your phone upright (portrait orientation) to fit the towers' full height, and step back as far as the pavement allows so the towers don't lean inwards. Wait for people and traffic to clear before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in the town of St. John's, on the island of Antigua. It sits close to Newgate Street. One guide says the only open gate is on Long Street, though street names around the cathedral may vary, so check on the day.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of St. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full west front with both towers. If you can't fit it all in from the pavement, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the tower tops, or to crop out scaffolding.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Newgate Street. The cathedral's west front and twin towers seen from the street, the classic postcard framing of the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the central axis of the façade up with a vertical grid line, so both towers sit evenly. Hold the phone level and upright, and keep the top of the towers just inside the frame. For a more atmospheric alternative, take a second shot in the grounds and old cemetery park, using the tombstones and greenery in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case people or traffic wander in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people in the street.

text.access_note: The street view is from a public street, but the grounds may only be open through one gate and the church may restrict photography during services, so check the official site before you go.

name: Dickenson Bay
label: Dickenson Bay
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Siboney Beach Club' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Siboney Beach Hotel' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5273629: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Antigua's most popular long white-sand resort beach.

text.description:
Dickenson Bay is a white-sand beach on Antigua's northwest coast with tranquil seas, which makes it an easy place to take good phone photos. The beachfront is busy in a pleasant way, lined with resort hotels, restaurants, beach bars and water sports stands. The bay has one of the island's largest collections of hotel rooms, so you will rarely have the sand to yourself. Offshore there are a few small uninhabited islands and a coral reef about a mile long.

The most popular photo here is the red British telephone box standing on the sand in front of Siboney Beach Club. With palm trees and turquoise sea behind it, it makes a cheerful portrait or landmark shot. The box no longer works, and one visitor found it covered up, so look at it before you set up a shot. Its exact position can differ between guides, so check the spot on the map.

If the phone box is not visible, or you want a second shot, try the Warri Pier for the curve of the shoreline and the sea at sunset. You could also try the beach in front of the Kon Tiki sign, where the bar sits out on the water. Both are older tips, so confirm locally that they are open to visitors. Walk a little way along the sand and take a few frames from different angles. The bay looks quite different with a person in the foreground.
text.geographic_location: Dickenson Bay lies on the northwest coast of Antigua, near McKinnon's. Runaway Beach is on the same bay.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed nearby, so check locally how to reach the beach from McKinnon's. Look for Siboney Beach Club on Dickenson Bay; the phone box stands on the sand in front of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the phone box with the palms and sea behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of the bay, and to the telephoto (2x) if you want a tighter, cleaner frame of the box without other beachgoers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Siboney Beach Club (on the beach in front of the club, with the red telephone box on the sand). The classic postcard frame: the red British phone box on the white sand, with palm trees and turquoise sea behind it. The wider bay stretches away to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the phone box on one third, leaving the sea and sky for the rest of the frame. Crouch slightly so the box stands out against the water rather than the sand. Keep the horizon level. For a second view, try the Warri Pier running out over the water, or the beach in front of the Kon Tiki sign.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the phone box to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white sand does not turn grey and the sky keeps its colour. Portrait mode works well if you want a person in front of the box with the background softened.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives softer light on the sand and suits sunset shots from the pier. Midday sun on white sand can be harsh, so lower the exposure slider if you shoot then.

text.access_note: The beach itself is open sand, but confirm locally that the Warri Pier and the Kon Tiki are still open to visitors, and make sure the phone box is visible.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon light is softer on the sand than midday light.
Midday sun on white sand can look harsh and fool the phone's exposure.
The beach is open sand that visitors can walk along.
The bay is likely to have other people on the beach during the day.
